question_text: What is the time and space complexity of common sorting algorithms and which would you use for different scenarios?
correct_answer: QuickSort: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst, O(log n) space — best general purpose. MergeSort: O(n log n) guaranteed, O(n) space — use when stability needed or for linked lists. HeapSort: O(n log n), O(1) space — when memory is critical. TimSort (Python/Java default): O(n log n), handles nearly-sorted data excellently. Counting Sort: O(n+k) — only for integers with small range. For nearly-sorted data use Insertion Sort O(n).
key_points: QuickSort: O(n log n) avg, in-place, fastest in practice
MergeSort: stable, guaranteed O(n log n), O(n) space
TimSort: hybrid, handles real-world data best
Counting Sort: linear but only for bounded integers
tip: Interviewer favourite: why is QuickSort faster than MergeSort despite same big-O? Cache locality.

question_text: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
correct_answer: Floyd's cycle detection algorithm (Tortoise and Hare) uses two pointers: slow moves one step, fast moves two steps. If they meet, a cycle exists. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. To find the cycle start point, move one pointer to head and advance both one step at a time — they meet at the cycle entry. Hash set approach also works but uses O(n) space.
key_points: Floyd's algorithm: slow/fast pointer, O(n) time O(1) space
Fast and slow pointers meet inside the cycle
Cycle start: move one pointer to head, advance both by 1
Hash set approach: O(n) space alternative
tip: Mathematical proof: why they meet at cycle entry when pointer resets to head — worth knowing.

question_text: Explain the difference between BFS and DFS and when to use each.
correct_answer: BFS (Breadth-First Search) explores level by level using a queue — finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs, used for level order traversal. DFS (Depth-First Search) explores as deep as possible using a stack (or recursion) — used for cycle detection, topological sort, finding all paths, and tree traversals (inorder, preorder, postorder). BFS memory is O(width) — bad for wide graphs. DFS memory is O(height).
key_points: BFS: queue, level-by-level, shortest unweighted path
DFS: stack/recursion, depth-first, cycle detection
BFS O(V+E) time, O(width) space
DFS O(V+E) time, O(height) space
tip: Use BFS for shortest path, DFS for maze solving/pathfinding when any path is OK.

question_text: What is dynamic programming and how do you identify when to use it?
correct_answer: Dynamic programming solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing results to avoid recomputation. Two signs you need DP: optimal substructure (optimal solution built from optimal subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (same subproblem computed multiple times). Top-down DP uses memoization (recursion + cache). Bottom-up DP builds the solution iteratively (often more space-efficient). Classic examples: Fibonacci, Knapsack, Longest Common Subsequence.
key_points: Overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure = DP
Memoization: top-down recursion with cache
Tabulation: bottom-up iterative, usually more efficient
State definition is the hardest part — define clearly
tip: The key insight: if the recursive solution recomputes the same arguments, add memoization.

question_text: How does a hash map work internally and what happens during collision?
correct_answer: A hash map computes a hash of the key, applies modulo to find bucket index, and stores (key, value) there. Collisions (two keys mapping to same bucket) are resolved by chaining (linked list at bucket) or open addressing (probe to next empty slot). Java HashMap uses chaining that converts to Red-Black tree when bucket size exceeds 8. Load factor (default 0.75) triggers resize — new array double size, all keys rehashed.
key_points: Hash(key) % capacity = bucket index
Chaining: linked list at each bucket
Open addressing: probe next empty bucket
Load factor triggers resize and rehash
tip: Java 8 HashMap: chain converts to tree at length 8 — O(log n) instead of O(n) for bad hash functions.

question_text: Find the maximum subarray sum (Kadane's algorithm). Explain the approach.
correct_answer: Kadane's algorithm: maintain currentMax (best ending here) and globalMax. At each element: currentMax = max(element, currentMax + element). If adding to previous subarray gives less than starting fresh, restart. globalMax = max(globalMax, currentMax). This is O(n) time and O(1) space. Handle all-negative arrays by initializing globalMax to first element. This is a classic DP problem where the state is 'max subarray ending at index i'.
key_points: currentMax = max(element, currentMax + element)
Reset when starting fresh is better than extending
O(n) time, O(1) space
Handle all-negative: initialize to nums[0] not 0
tip: Draw the state transition clearly — decide at each step: start new subarray or extend existing one.

question_text: What is a binary search tree and what are its time complexities?
correct_answer: A BST is a binary tree where left child < parent < right child. Search, insert, delete are O(h) where h is height. For balanced BST, h = O(log n). Worst case (sorted input) degrades to O(n) — a linear chain. Self-balancing BSTs (AVL, Red-Black) maintain O(log n) operations. Inorder traversal of BST gives sorted output. Used for ordered sets, range queries, and as underlying structure in TreeMap/TreeSet.
key_points: left < node < right property
Operations: O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate
Self-balancing: AVL (strict), Red-Black (approximate)
Inorder traversal gives sorted sequence
tip: Construct a BST from sorted array — always pick middle as root to keep balanced.

question_text: Explain the two-pointer technique and give an example problem.
correct_answer: Two pointers maintain two indices simultaneously to scan through data. Useful for: finding pairs with target sum (sorted array), removing duplicates, reversing in-place, and partitioning. For sorted array pair sum: left pointer at start, right at end — if sum > target move right left, if sum < target move left right. This converts naive O(n²) nested loop to O(n). Three Sum extends this to O(n²) with outer loop + two pointers inside.
key_points: Left and right pointers converging from both ends
Sorted array is often required for convergence to work
O(n) vs naive O(n²) — linear improvement
Works for: pair sum, palindrome check, partition
tip: Two Sum sorted array: show how converging pointers eliminate pairs — elegant and O(n).

question_text: What is a heap (priority queue) and what problems does it solve efficiently?
correct_answer: A heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property: parent >= children (max-heap) or parent <= children (min-heap). Insert and extractMin/Max are O(log n). Find min/max is O(1). Built using an array with parent at i, left child at 2i+1, right at 2i+2. Used for: top K elements (min-heap of size K), merge K sorted lists, Dijkstra's algorithm, and scheduling problems. Python heapq implements min-heap.
key_points: Insert: O(log n), ExtractMin/Max: O(log n), Peek: O(1)
Array-based complete binary tree — cache friendly
Top K elements: maintain min-heap of size K
Dijkstra and Prim use min-heap for greedy selection
tip: Top K largest elements: use min-heap of size K — counter-intuitive but efficient O(n log K).

question_text: How would you check if a binary tree is a valid BST?
correct_answer: Do NOT just compare node with its direct children — a BST violation can occur with a distant ancestor. Pass min and max bounds recursively: root starts with (-∞, +∞). Left subtree must have values < root.val so pass (min, root.val). Right subtree must have values > root.val so pass (root.val, max). Each node checks min < node.val < max. Alternatively, inorder traversal should produce a strictly increasing sequence — check this iteratively.
key_points: Naive left/right comparison is wrong — ancestor bounds needed
Recursive: pass (min, max) bounds down the tree
Alternatively: inorder must be strictly increasing
Handle duplicates: BST definition usually requires strict inequality
tip: Common mistake: check only node vs children. Show the ancestor bound approach — interviewers test this.

question_text: What is the sliding window technique and when do you apply it?
correct_answer: The sliding window maintains a contiguous subarray or substring and expands/contracts it based on conditions. Fixed window: sum of K consecutive elements — slide one element. Variable window: longest substring without repeating — expand right, contract left when condition violated. This converts O(n²) nested loops to O(n). Common problems: max sum subarray of size K, longest substring with K distinct chars, minimum window substring.
key_points: Fixed window: move both pointers together
Variable window: expand right, shrink left on violation
HashMap tracks element frequency in window
O(n) — each element added and removed at most once
tip: Variable window pattern: right++ always, left++ when condition violated — clean template to memorize.

question_text: Explain merge sort and how you would implement it.
correct_answer: Merge sort recursively divides the array in half until base case (size 1), then merges sorted halves. Merge function compares elements from both halves and places smaller one into result array. O(n log n) guaranteed time, O(n) space for auxiliary array. Stable sort — preserves relative order of equal elements. Used in external sorting (large files) and when stability is required. Bottom-up merge sort avoids recursion stack overhead.
key_points: Divide: split in half recursively
Conquer: merge two sorted halves linearly
O(n log n) guaranteed — no worst case like QuickSort
Stable and works on linked lists without random access
tip: Merge step is the key — two pointer merge into temp array, handle remaining elements.

question_text: What is topological sorting and where is it used?
correct_answer: Topological sort orders vertices in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) such that for every edge u→v, u comes before v. Kahn's algorithm: track in-degrees, start with 0 in-degree nodes, process and reduce neighbors' in-degrees, add newly zero in-degree nodes to queue. DFS approach: add node to stack after visiting all its descendants. Used for: build systems (dependencies), course scheduling, task ordering, and compilation order.
key_points: Only works on DAGs — cycles have no valid ordering
Kahn's algorithm: BFS with in-degree tracking
DFS: add to result after exploring all descendants
If all nodes not processed → cycle detected
tip: Course Schedule problem on LeetCode — perfect topological sort application to practice.

question_text: How does Dijkstra's algorithm work and what are its limitations?
correct_answer: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from source to all vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edges. Maintains a min-heap of (distance, vertex) pairs. Extract minimum distance vertex, relax all edges from it, add updated neighbors to heap. O((V+E) log V) with binary heap. Limitation: does not work with negative edge weights — use Bellman-Ford for that. Also does not work for detecting negative cycles.
key_points: Greedy: always process closest unvisited vertex
Min-heap for efficient extraction of minimum
O((V+E) log V) with binary heap
Fails with negative edges — use Bellman-Ford instead
tip: Dijkstra greedy works because non-negative edges guarantee a visited node's shortest path is final.

question_text: What is the difference between a stack and a queue and what algorithms use them?
correct_answer: Stack is LIFO (Last In First Out) — push/pop from same end. Queue is FIFO (First In First Out) — enqueue at back, dequeue from front. Stack algorithms: DFS graph traversal, function call stack, balanced parentheses, monotonic stack problems, undo/redo. Queue algorithms: BFS graph traversal, level-order tree traversal, sliding window maximum (monotonic deque). Deque (double-ended queue) supports both stack and queue operations.
key_points: Stack: LIFO, used for DFS and recursion simulation
Queue: FIFO, used for BFS and level-order traversal
Monotonic stack: O(n) solution for next greater element
Deque: both ends, sliding window max in O(n)
tip: Implement a queue using two stacks — classic interview question testing data structure understanding.

question_text: What is Big O notation and how do you analyze algorithm complexity?
correct_answer: Big O notation describes the upper bound of an algorithm's time or space growth as input size n approaches infinity. Drop constants and lower-order terms: O(2n + 5) = O(n). Common complexities: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2^n) < O(n!). Analyze loops: single = O(n), nested = O(n²). Recursive: use recurrence relations (T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n → O(n log n) for merge sort). Space complexity counts auxiliary memory used.
key_points: Drop constants and non-dominant terms
Nested loops multiply complexities
Recursion: use Master Theorem or recurrence tree
Best/average/worst case — O is worst case bound
tip: O(log n) always means the input is being halved — binary search, balanced BST operations.
